title: Ensure health and safety in the perishable produce export environment

lessons.title: Legal duties and hazards in packhouses and cold stores
lessons.html:
The law

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 (OHS Act) applies to farms, packhouses, cold stores and transport depots. Under the Act:

  • The employer must provide and maintain, as far as reasonably practicable, a working environment that is safe and without risk to health. This includes safe machinery, training, supervision and protective equipment.
  • Employees must take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others, follow safety rules, use protective equipment and report unsafe conditions and incidents.
  • Workplaces above a certain size must appoint health and safety representatives and may need a health and safety committee.

Injured workers are covered by the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 (COIDA), which requires employers to register and to report injuries.

Common hazards in the export environment

AreaHazards
Packing lineMoving belts, rollers and brushes that trap fingers, hair and clothing; noise; repetitive strain
Forklifts and pallet jacksCollisions with people, falling loads, overturning
Cold storesCold stress, slippery floors, being locked in, poor visibility
Refrigeration plantAmmonia leaks in many large systems: toxic and irritating gas
ChemicalsFungicides, sanitisers, cleaning agents, fuels: splashes, fumes, skin contact
Loading baysTrucks reversing, falls from docks, gaps between dock and truck
StackingCollapsing pallets, manual lifting of heavy cartons
ElectricalDamaged cables, wet areas, generators

A supervisor must know where these hazards are in their area and make sure controls are in place before work starts each day. A short walk-through at the start of each shift, checking guards, walkways, cold store door releases and the chemical store, catches most problems before anyone is hurt.

lessons.title: Controls, safe work and emergencies
lessons.html:
Risk assessment and control

For each task, identify the hazard, judge how likely and how serious the harm could be, and put controls in place. Use the order of controls: eliminate the hazard, substitute something safer, use engineering controls (guards, interlocks), use administrative controls (procedures, training, signs) and, last, personal protective equipment (PPE).

Safe work rules

  • Machinery: guards always in place; never reach into a moving machine; lock out and tag out power before cleaning or repairs.
  • Forklifts: only trained, authorised drivers; pedestrian walkways marked; never carry passengers; never lift people on forks.
  • Cold stores: wear issued thermal clothing; limit time in very cold rooms; doors must open from inside and have alarm or release systems; tell someone before entering.
  • Chemicals: follow the label and safety data sheet; wear the specified gloves, goggles or respirator; store in a locked, ventilated store; never decant into cooldrink bottles.
  • Manual handling: bend the knees, keep the load close, get help for heavy loads and use pallet jacks.
  • Housekeeping: keep floors dry and clear; clean up spills immediately.

Emergencies

  • Ammonia leak: the sharp smell is a warning. Raise the alarm, evacuate upwind to the assembly point, and never re-enter without trained responders and proper breathing apparatus.
  • Fire: raise the alarm, evacuate, and only fight a small fire with the correct extinguisher if trained and safe. Keep fire exits and extinguishers unobstructed.
  • Injury: call the trained first aider and emergency services. Do not move a seriously injured person unless they are in danger. For chemical splashes in the eyes, rinse with clean running water for a long time and get medical help.

First aid must be given by trained first aiders. Hands-on training by an accredited provider is required before anyone acts as a first aider.

Reporting and records

Report all incidents and near misses to the supervisor. Record them, investigate the cause and fix it. Serious incidents must be reported to the authorities as the law requires.

Key points

  • The OHS Act places duties on both employer and employees.
  • Major hazards include machinery, forklifts, cold stores, ammonia and chemicals.
  • Use the order of controls, with PPE as the last line of defence.
  • Lock out machines before cleaning; only trained drivers operate forklifts.
  • Know emergency procedures and report all incidents and near misses.
